purpose: Penicillin G is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections such as strep throat, syphilis, pneumonia, meningitis, and certain heart infections. Your doctor may also use it to prevent infections in people who are at high risk. It only works against bacterial infections — it will not help with colds, flu, or other viral illnesses.
how_it_works: Penicillin G works by attacking the outer wall that surrounds bacteria. Bacteria need this wall to survive, and when the wall breaks down, the bacteria die. Think of it like removing the protective shell of the germ — without it, the bacteria cannot hold together and your body can clear the infection.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach upset. You may also notice pain, redness, or soreness at the injection site since this medicine is given as a shot. Some people develop a mild skin rash.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have any signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, or a severe rash — these can be life-threatening. Let your doctor know if you have ever had a reaction to penicillin or any other antibiotic before starting this medicine. If you have kidney problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. Always finish the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better.
typical_dosing: Penicillin G is given as an injection either into a muscle or into a vein — it is not taken by mouth in pill form. The dose and how often you receive it depends on the type and seriousness of your infection. Some forms are given as a single shot, while others may be given every few hours in a hospital setting. Your doctor or nurse will determine the right dose for you.
